title: Why a rocket that learned to fly could not learn to hover
paper_title: RocketSim: Benchmarking Reinforcement-Learning Hover Control of a Reusable Booster
date_note: Information Society 2026 multiconference, Ljubljana, early October 2026 (proceedings Vol. 1, pp. 64-67); exact day approximate
authors: Swarnendu Ghosh, David Muhič, Branko Šter
summary: A short guide to the RocketSim paper: a learning agent kept a booster upright but could not hold its height, and why. The full write-up is on the LANCER project page.
cta: Read the full write-up on the LANCER page

body.p: This paper is part of LANCER, my research project at the University of Ljubljana on teaching autonomous vehicles to navigate difficult environments with reinforcement learning, meaning learning by trial and error against a reward. Most of the project is about cars. This paper steps sideways to a rocket booster, because a rocket makes one problem very visible: what happens when the reward does not tell the learner clearly what you want.

Studies of reusable rockets usually ask a learning agent to land. Landing gives it a clear goal: touch down gently. We asked something harder to define. Release a booster at 80 metres and ask it to hold 30 metres above the pad. Nothing special happens at 30 metres, so there is no moment that says “well done”. We built a simulator called RocketSim in the Unity game engine and trained a standard algorithm, PPO, to do it.

figure.alt: Five test flights of one trained agent: the plan views show tight lateral control while the altitude traces sag below the 30 metre target, approach the ground, then climb to the ceiling.
figure.caption: Five test flights of the same trained agent. It stays over the pad, but its height drifts from near the ground to the ceiling.

body.p: The agent learned to stay upright, stay over the pad and keep flying until its fuel ran out. It did not learn to hold the height. With nothing changed except the random seed, the average height error across five training runs ranged from 24 to 105 metres, even though their scores were within 10% of each other.

We found two separate causes. The reward barely changes with height unless the rocket is very close to the target, so the learner has nothing to follow. And the engine cannot throttle below 39% of its power, so once the booster is lighter than 33.6 tonnes, no setting can hold it in place for the last 55% of the burn. We tried to repair both. Reshaping the reward cut the average error from 36 to 6 metres but still stranded one run in five.
The lesson: hovering has to be fixed in the reward and in the vehicle together. The project page has the rest.
